title: Comments of Ransom Township Municipal Building on the Pre-Application Document and Notice of Intent re the proposed Old Forge Bore Hole Pumped Storage Project under P-15411.

documents.name: VIA FERC EFILE 10.5.2026.pdf
documents.text:
VIA FERC E-FILING

Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary,
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, NE
Washington, DC 20426

RE: Old Forge Pumped Storage Project, Project No. P-15411-001Comments of
Ransom Township, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania, Regarding the Notice of
Intent (NOI), Pre-Application Document (PAD), and Request for the Integrated
Licensing Process (ILP)

Dear Secretary Reese,

The Board of Supervisors of Ransom Township, Lackawanna County, Pennsylvania,
respectfully submits these comments regarding the Pre-Application Document (PAD) and
Notice of Intent (NOI) filed by Renewable Energy Aggregators, Inc. for the proposed Old
Forge Pumped Storage Project (Project No. P-15411-001).A substantial portion of the
proposed 1,300-acre project boundary and its primary infrastructure, including massive
reservoir within Agricultural and Open Space/Conservation Zoning Districts, natural gas
generation units, and connecting pipelines, falls directly within the borders of Ransom
Township. As a rural community heavily dependent on the protection of its natural
topography and residential zoning, Ransom Township expresses severe concerns
regarding the scale, environmental hazards, and localized disruptions presented by this
project. Under the Integrated Licensing Process (ILP), Ransom Township requests that
the Commission compel the applicant to perform rigorous, independent, and exhaustive
environmental, engineering, and socioeconomic studies on the following matters before
a final license application is considered:

1. Scope of Municipal Notification and Lack of Consultation
Ransom Township formally objects to any prior characterizations that have sidelined our
local government from early formal notices or consultations under the assumption of our
smaller population size. Because our township bears the physical burden of the proposed
footprint, we request that Ransom Township be explicitly integrated as a core consulting
local agency in all upcoming scoping meetings, site visits, and study plan developments.
 2. Critical Risk to Public Health and Private Water Supply
Ransom Township possesses absolutely no municipal or public water supply
infrastructure. Every household, farm, and business within our borders relies entirely on
private groundwater wells for drinking water and daily consumption. The applicant's
proposal to move, agitate, and store millions of gallons of toxic acid mine drainage (AMD)
from local boreholes into massive reservoirs within Agricultural and Open
Space/Conservation Zoning Districts poses an existential threat to our residents' public
health. Any subterranean leaching, bedrock fracturing of existing mine voids, or systemic
groundwater table disturbance could permanently contaminate or collapse our township's
sole drinking water source. We demand a mandatory, long-term independent hydrological
impact study, alongside a binding baseline testing and monitoring framework for all
private residential wells within a multi-mile radius of the project.


3. Incompatibility with Rural Infrastructure and Local Road Constraints
The transportation network throughout Ransom Township consists strictly of narrow,
rural, non-highway local roads. These secondary corridors are designed for low-volume
residential traffic and agricultural use, not heavy industrial payloads. They possess
neither the structural grading, lane widths, nor geometric configurations necessary to
sustain continuous, multi-year industrial construction vehicles. The introduction of heavy
machinery, multi-ton equipment hauling, and extensive workforce transit will rapidly
degrade our road surfaces, compromise local bridges, and create severe public safety
hazards for emergency response vehicles. FERC must require a comprehensive Traffic
Impact Assessment and compel the applicant to enter into a legally binding infrastructure
mitigation and road maintenance agreement with Ransom Township before any permit or
license approval moves forward.

4. Zoning Preemption, Land Use, and Property Value Devaluation
While federal licensing under FERC can preempt local zoning, the Commission must
evaluate the extensive harm this project poses to Ransom Township’s master land use
plans and the property values of our adjacent residents. The construction of massive
reservoirs, industrial piping, and a 200-megawatt natural gas generator directly conflicts
with our rural zoning character. The applicant must be required to provide a complete
property impact study detailing how industrial noise pollution, visual blights on the
mountain ridge, and construction vibrations will impact surrounding residential
landowners.

5. Ecological Fragmentation and Mountain Wildlife Impacts
Contrary to statements suggesting an absence of wildlife in the targeted mountain and
ridge areas, the area hosts thriving, diverse ecosystems. Clearing large swaths of
forestland will cause severe wildlife habitat fragmentation, disrupt native migratory
species, and increase rainwater runoff and soil erosion down the mountain slopes.
Ransom Township requests multi-season ecological and biodiversity studies to fully map
the environmental toll of the footprint.
 6. Cumulative Infrastructure Impacts (Data Center Speculation)
Publicly available documentation and local community consensus indicate that this power
infrastructure is intended to supply massive data center developments in the immediate
vicinity. Ransom Township urges FERC to expand its NEPA review to include a
cumulative impact assessment of both the pumped storage facility and any secondary,
interdependent high-density industrial data facilities being planned concurrently.

Conclusion: Ransom Township strongly urges the Commission to prioritize the health,
safety, and property rights of our residents during the Integrated Licensing Process. The
applicant must not be allowed to fast-track a project that threatens to fundamentally alter
our Township's environment and ruin our essential local infrastructure without satisfying
a strict, transparent, and multi-year environmental study plan.Thank you for your time and
careful consideration of our community's concerns.

                                                 Respectfully submitted,


                                                 David Bird
                                                 Chairman, Board of Supervisors
                                                 Ransom Township, Pennsylvania
